lead: A key is a small steel piece that sits in matching slots in a shaft and a hub, so the shaft can drive a gear, pulley or coupling without slipping. The slot is the keyway. A spline does the same job with many teeth cut on the shaft, so it carries more torque and can let the hub slide. A key is sized from two checks, shear and crushing, and the keyway it needs weakens the shaft, so both are part of shaft design. Every motor, pump, gearbox and bicycle crank uses one.
prereq: You need: torque and shaft diameter from shafts under bending, torsion and axial loads.

items: Sunk keys sit half in the shaft and half in the hub. A rectangular key has width w = d/4 and height h = 2w/3 (the common case); a square key has h = w = d/4. A parallel key has no taper; a taper key has a 1 in 100 taper on its top and is driven in, often with a gib head so it can be pulled out.
A feather key is a parallel key fixed to the shaft or hub so the hub can slide along the shaft, as for a gear-shift clutch.
A Woodruff key is a half disc in a curved seat. It tilts to match a tapered shaft end and is common in machine tools and car engines, but its deep seat weakens the shaft.
Saddle keys (flat or hollow) need no shaft keyway and drive by friction only, so they suit light loads.

Tangent keys are a pair of taper keys at 90° for heavy reversing torque, as on flywheels. A round key is a pin in a drilled hole for small torque. A Kennedy key is a pair of square keys set diagonally for heavy duty.

blocks.text: Key widths and heights come from standard tables for each shaft range; for a 44 to 50 mm shaft the standard rectangular key is 14 mm × 9 mm. The key fits snugly on its sides and has a small clearance at the top, so the torque passes through the side faces.

sections.h3: Forces and stresses in a sunk key

blocks.text: The torque T reaches the key as a tangential force at the shaft surface: F = 2T/d. That force can fail the key in two ways.

items: Shear across the plane where shaft and hub meet: area wl, so τ = F/(wl) = 2T/(dwl).
Crushing of the side face: half the height bears on the hub, area (h/2)l, so σc = F/((h/2)l) = 4T/(dhl).

blocks.text: Here l is the key length in contact with the hub. Design takes the larger length from the two checks and makes the hub at least that long. The hub is often of cast iron, so its keyway is checked for crushing with the hub’s own allowable stress. For a square key in a material whose crushing strength is twice its shear strength, the two checks give the same length. Making the key as strong as the shaft in shear (wlτd/2 = πd³τ/16) gives l = πd²/(8w), which is 1.571d for w = d/4: that is why key lengths of about 1.5d are common.

sections.h3: Effect of the keyway, and splines

blocks.text: A keyway removes metal and leaves sharp corners, so the shaft is weaker. Moore’s formula gives the strength factor of a keyed shaft compared with a plain one: e = 1 − 0.2(w/d) − 1.1(h1/d), where h1 is the keyway depth in the shaft (about h/2). A round-ended (profile) keyway cut by an end mill has a higher stress-concentration factor than a sled-runner keyway cut by a disc cutter. The ASME code covers any keyway with a 25 % lower allowable stress.

A spline shaft has several (often 4, 6, 10 or 16) teeth cut on it. Straight-sided splines have parallel flanks; involute splines have gear-like flanks that centre themselves and are stronger. A sliding fit lets the hub move along the shaft, as in a gearbox; a fixed fit does not. The torque capacity follows from the side-face pressure: T = p n h l Rm, where n is the number of splines, h = (D − d)/2 the tooth height, l the engaged length and Rm = (D + d)/4 the mean radius. Splines spread the load and avoid one deep keyway, so they carry more torque in the same space.

examples.question: A 50 mm shaft transmits 20 kW at 600 rpm through a standard 14 mm × 9 mm rectangular sunk key. The key steel has allowable shear stress 40 MPa and allowable crushing stress 80 MPa. Find the key length, and the strength factor of the keyed shaft taking the keyway depth as h/2.
steps: Force at the shaft surface: F = 2T/d = 2 × 318 310/50 = 12 732 N.
Length for shear: l = F/(wτ) = 12 732/(14 × 40) = 22.7 mm.
Length for crushing: l = F/((h/2)σ<sub>c</sub>) = 12 732/(4.5 × 80) = 35.4 mm.
Crushing governs. Adopt l = 40 mm; then τ = 12 732/(14 × 40) = 22.7 MPa and σ<sub>c</sub> = 12 732/(4.5 × 40) = 70.7 MPa, both within limits.
examples.answer: Key 14 × 9 × 40 mm. The keyway leaves the shaft with about 84.5 % of the strength of a plain 50 mm shaft.

traps: Using the full height h for crushing. Only half the key bears on the hub, so the area is (h/2)l.
Taking the key force as T/d. It acts at the shaft surface: F = T/(d/2) = 2T/d.
Checking only shear. A rectangular key usually needs more length for crushing, as in the worked example.
Choosing a key longer than the hub. The length that counts is the length in contact with the hub.
Calling a Woodruff key the strongest. Its deep seat weakens the shaft most; it is chosen for easy assembly on tapered ends.

quiz.a: Rectangular or square sunk key, gib-head taper key, feather key, Woodruff key, saddle key (also tangent, round and Kennedy keys).

quiz.q: Write the standard proportions of a rectangular sunk key.
quiz.a: Width w = d/4 and height h = 2w/3 = d/6, where d is the shaft diameter.

quiz.q: Why is a saddle key used only for light loads?
quiz.a: It has no keyway in the shaft and drives only by the friction between its curved face and the shaft, so a high or shock torque makes it slip.

quiz.q: What is a feather key and where is it used?
quiz.a: A parallel key fixed to the shaft or the hub with a sliding fit in the other part, so the hub can move along the shaft while turning with it; for example a sliding gear or a dog clutch.

quiz.q: A 40 mm shaft transmits 10 kW at 900 rpm. The key is 12 mm wide and 50 mm long. Find the shear stress in the key.
A shaft has 6 straight-sided splines with D = 50 mm, d = 46 mm and an engaged length of 60 mm. The allowable side pressure is 6.5 MPa. Find the torque capacity.
Why does a keyway shorten a shaft’s fatigue life even when the key itself is strong enough?
quiz.a: The keyway removes metal and leaves sharp root corners. The local stress at the corners is two to three times the nominal stress, and under repeated torsion and bending a crack starts there. A larger root fillet, a sled-runner keyway or splines reduce this.

beyond: Key and keyway sizes come from national standards tables, and designers check the keyed shaft with fatigue stress-concentration factors from handbooks. Involute splines are standardised by module and pressure angle like gears; cars use them on drive shafts and gearbox mainshafts. Keyless locking devices (taper rings) are replacing keys where the shaft must not be weakened. Search for "involute spline standard" and "keyless shaft locking device".

figure.caption: Section through the keyed shaft of the worked example. The torque pushes the hub and shaft against opposite sides of the key: the key can shear on the plane at the shaft surface (area w × l) or crush on the half height h/2 that sits in the hub. Crushing needs the longer key, 35.4 mm.
